methods.title: Margin of error for a difference → cutoff × standard error
methods.trigger: A report gives a difference "plus or minus" some amount, or asks for the half-width of a 95% interval for two means or two proportions.

methods.title: Hormone therapy and study design → relative risk and chi-square
methods.trigger: A 2×2 table compares deaths in a treated and an untreated group, and the question asks for the relative risk or whether the death rates differ, or what the study design allows.

methods.title: Simple regression review → comparing two slopes
methods.trigger: Two independent groups each have a regression line (slope and standard error), and the question asks whether the relationship differs between the groups.

methods.title: Multiple regression fit → b = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy and s_y|x
methods.trigger: Several independent variables predict one continuous outcome, and the question asks for the coefficients, the fitted equation, or the variability about the fitted plane.

methods.title: Multiple regression tests → F for the model, t for each coefficient
methods.trigger: An R summary() of a multiple regression is given and the question asks whether the model as a whole, or each variable, is significant, or asks for a prediction or a coefficient interval.

methods.title: Logistic regression → probability, logit and odds
methods.trigger: The outcome is yes or no (present or absent), and the question asks how its probability depends on one or more variables, or for a probability or odds at a given value.

cases.title: Margin of error for a two-group survey difference
cases.context: Original practice example. A campus survey asks first-year and senior students whether they use a campus fitness facility at least weekly. A news summary reports the difference in percentage points "plus or minus" a margin of error. Use the Session 17 pooled-proportion standard error and the Normal cutoff.
tasks: Find both sample proportions and their difference, first-year minus senior.
Calculate the pooled standard error and the 95% margin of error \(z_{0.05}s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\).
Report the result in survey style (difference plus or minus the margin) and decide whether the difference is significant at the two-sided 0.05 level.

hypotheses.nullWords: First-year and senior students use the facility weekly in equal proportions.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The weekly-use proportions of first-year and senior students differ.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (yes answers), \(n_i\) (respondents), \(\hat p_i\) (sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled proportion), \(s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\) (SE of the difference), \(z_{0.05}\) (two-sided Normal cutoff), \(M\) (margin of error).

steps.title: Find both sample proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the number of yes answers divided by the number of respondents in that group.

steps.title: Find the observed difference
steps.words: Keep the direction first-year minus senior throughout.

steps.title: Pool the two groups
steps.words: The Session 17 convention pools both groups to estimate one common proportion for the standard error.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: Multiply the pooled variance term by the sum of the reciprocal group sizes, then take the root.

steps.title: Read the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, and use the infinity row in the 0.05 two-tail column. The infinity row is the standard Normal cutoff, 1.960.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error
steps.words: This product is the number a survey report prints after "plus or minus".

steps.title: Form the interval and decide
steps.words: Zero lies outside the interval because the observed difference is larger than its margin of error, so reject equal proportions at the two-sided 0.05 level.

cases.conclusion: The first-year minus senior difference is 10.0 percentage points plus or minus 6.23 points (95% CI 0.0377 to 0.1623). Zero is excluded, so first-year students use the facility weekly in a higher proportion (P < 0.05).

cases.title: Hormone replacement therapy and mortality
cases.context: Glantz problem 5-13 (Grodstein and colleagues, 1997) compares deaths among postmenopausal women currently using hormone replacement therapy with deaths among women who never used it. The groups are defined by use, not by random assignment.
tasks: Test whether the death rate differs between the two groups with a chi-square test (Yates correction for the 2×2 table). State the hypotheses in words.
Calculate the relative risk of dying, hormone group relative to never-used group, and interpret it.
State what this comparison can and cannot show, given how the groups were formed.

hypotheses.nullWords: The death rate is the same for current hormone users and never-users.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The death rate differs between current hormone users and never-users.

cases.symbols: \(n_{TD}\) (deaths in the hormone group), \(n_T\) (hormone group size), \(n_{CD}\) (deaths in the never-used group), \(n_C\) (never-used group size), \(O\) (observed count), \(E\) (expected count), \(RR\) (relative risk).

steps.title: Find the group totals
steps.words: Add deaths and survivors in each row. The grand total is 28628.

steps.title: Calculate expected counts
steps.words: Expected counts are what each cell would hold if the death rate were the same in both groups.

steps.title: Calculate the Yates-corrected chi-square
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute discrepancy before squaring, as the course does for 2×2 tables.

steps.title: Compare with the chi-square cutoff
steps.words: Open Chi_Squared_Table1.pdf, page 1, row 1. The 0.05 column gives 3.841 and the 0.001 column gives 10.828. The statistic exceeds both, so reject with P < 0.001.

steps.title: Calculate both death proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the risk of dying within that group.

steps.title: Calculate the relative risk
steps.words: The risk of dying in the hormone group is about 60% of the risk in the never-used group.

steps.title: State what the design allows
steps.words: Women were grouped by whether they used hormones, not assigned at random, so the result is an association. The later randomized WHI trial on the next page reached a less favorable overall conclusion.

cases.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis (chi-square = 127.06, 1 df, P < 0.001): the death rate differs between current hormone users and never-users. The relative risk is 0.6047, so the hormone group's risk of dying is about 60% of the never-used group's risk in this non-randomized comparison.

cases.title: Plutonian weight on height: males versus females
cases.context: Lecture exercise. Separate R regressions of weight (lbs) on height (inches) are run for 18 male and 18 female Plutonians. Test whether the slopes of the two lines of means differ. The slope standard errors come from the R output.
tasks: State the null and alternative hypotheses for equal slopes in symbols and words.
Calculate the standard error of the slope difference and the t statistic.
Find the degrees of freedom and the critical value from the printed t table, decide, and give the P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: The mean weight of male and female Plutonians increases with height at the same rate.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which mean weight increases with height differs between male and female Plutonians.

cases.symbols: \(b_M, b_F\) (sample slopes), \(s_{b_M}, s_{b_F}\) (slope standard errors), \(s_{b_M-b_F}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Read both slopes and standard errors
steps.words: Take the Height.in row of each R coefficient table: the Estimate column and the Std. Error column.

steps.title: Calculate the slope difference
steps.words: Males gain about 1.25 lbs more per inch of height than females in these samples.

steps.title: Calculate the SE of the difference
steps.words: The two samples are independent, so the variances of the two slopes add.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Divide the slope difference by its standard error.

steps.title: Find df and the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 32, two-tail 0.05 column: 2.037. Four degrees of freedom are lost because each line estimates an intercept and a slope.

steps.title: Decide and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic exceeds the 0.05 cutoff but not the 0.02 cutoff of 2.449, so 0.02 < P < 0.05.

cases.conclusion: Reject equal slopes (t = 2.444, 32 df, 0.02 < P < 0.05). Mean weight rises faster with height in male Plutonians (3.2833 lbs/in) than in female Plutonians (2.029 lbs/in).

cases.title: Child SBP on mother and father SBP: least squares by matrix
cases.context: Hypertension in families (Rosner). Twenty families give the systolic blood pressure (mm Hg) of the first-born child (y), the mother (x1) and the father (x2). Fit the multiple regression by the matrix least-squares formula and confirm the R estimates.
tasks: Build \(X^TX\) and \(X^Ty\) from the sums of the data.
Solve \(b=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\) for \(b_0, b_1, b_2\).
Use \(SS_{res}\) to find \(s_{y|x}\) and \(R^2\).
cases.symbols: \(X\) (design matrix: a column of ones, then x1 and x2), \(y\) (child SBP vector), \(b\) (coefficient vector), \(SS_{res}\) (sum of squared residuals), \(SS_{tot}\) (total sum of squares), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error).

steps.title: Build the cross-product matrix
general: X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}n&\sum x_1&\sum x_2\\\sum x_1&\sum x_1^2&\sum x_1x_2\\\sum x_2&\sum x_1x_2&\sum x_2^2\end{bmatrix}
steps.words: Each entry is a sum over the 20 families; the first row and column come from the column of ones.

steps.title: Build the cross-product vector
steps.words: Multiply each column of X by the child SBP values and add.

steps.title: Invert the cross-product matrix
steps.words: The inverse is found with software; its diagonal entries are reused later for the coefficient standard errors.

steps.title: Solve for the coefficients
steps.words: These match the R Estimate column: -15.6892, 0.4225 and 0.4150.

steps.title: Calculate the residual variance
steps.words: Three parameters are estimated, so 17 degrees of freedom remain. The root is the Residual standard error that R prints as 10.67.

steps.title: Calculate R squared
steps.words: About 60% of the variation in child SBP is accounted for by the two parental SBPs together; R prints Multiple R-squared 0.5973.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares plane is ŷ = -15.69 + 0.4225x1 + 0.4150x2 (mm Hg), with s_y|x = 10.67 mm Hg on 17 df and R² = 0.5973, matching the R summary.

cases.title: Reading the R summary for child SBP
cases.context: The R call lm(SBPchild ~ SBPmother + SBPfather) on the 20 families prints the summary below. Use it to test the model as a whole, test each parental coefficient, and predict by hand.
tasks: Test \(H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0\) with the F statistic. Recompute F from R², give the critical value from the printed F table, and conclude.
Test each parental coefficient with \(t=b_j/s_{b_j}\) and the printed t table; give 95% intervals for both slopes.
Predict the mean SBP of a first-born child whose mother has SBP 130 mm Hg and father 150 mm Hg.

hypotheses.nullWords: Neither the mother's nor the father's SBP is related to the child's mean SBP.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: At least one parent's SBP is related to the child's mean SBP.

cases.symbols: \(R^2\) (multiple R-squared), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(n\) (number of families), \(MS_{mod}, MS_{res}\) (model and residual mean squares), \(b_j\) (coefficient), \(s_{b_j}\) (its standard error).

steps.title: Find the F degrees of freedom
steps.words: Two independent variables are tested together; 17 degrees of freedom remain for the residuals.

steps.title: Recompute F from R squared
steps.words: Dividing SS_mod and SS_res by SS_tot turns them into R² and 1 − R², so F can be checked from the printed R². R prints 12.61.

steps.title: Compare with the F cutoff
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, page 1: numerator column 2, denominator row 17. The lightface value is 3.59 and the boldface value is 6.11. F exceeds both, so P < 0.01 from the table; R gives P = 0.0004388 (P < 0.001).

steps.title: Test the mother coefficient
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 17: 2.110 at 0.05. The statistic also lies between 3.222 (0.005) and 3.646 (0.002), so 0.002 < P < 0.005, matching R's 0.00238.

steps.title: Test the father coefficient
steps.words: The father coefficient is also significant; 3.325 lies between 3.222 and 3.646, so 0.002 < P < 0.005, matching R's 0.00401.

steps.title: Build 95% intervals for both slopes
steps.words: Neither interval contains zero, which agrees with both t tests.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute the parental SBPs into the fitted plane; the result is a mean child SBP in mm Hg.

cases.conclusion: Reject H0 (F = 12.61 on 2 and 17 df, P < 0.001 from R; P < 0.01 from the printed table). The mother's and father's SBPs together predict the child's SBP, and each is significant on its own (t = 3.565 and 3.325, 0.002 < P < 0.005). The predicted mean child SBP for parents at 130 and 150 mm Hg is 101.5 mm Hg.

cases.title: Six-minute walk distance: summary, confint, refit and prediction
cases.context: Original practice example in the style of an R multiple-regression exercise. For 32 adults in a rehabilitation program, six-minute walk distance (m) is regressed on Age (years), BMI (kg/m²) and Exercise (hours per week). R prints the summary(), the confint() output, and a refit with only the significant variables.
tasks: Write the full regression equation and test \(H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0\) with the F statistic.
Decide which variables are significant from the t tests, then confirm with the confint() intervals.
Refit with the significant variables only and predict the walk distance of a 68-year-old who exercises 4.5 hours per week, by hand.

hypotheses.nullWords: BMI has no relation to mean walk distance once age and exercise are in the model.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: BMI is related to mean walk distance once age and exercise are in the model.

cases.symbols: \(b_j\) (coefficient estimate), \(s_{b_j}\) (standard error), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(\nu=n-k-1\) (residual degrees of freedom), \(\hat y\) (predicted mean distance).

steps.title: Write the full equation
steps.words: Read the Estimate column of the full summary.

steps.title: Test the model as a whole
steps.words: F_table.pdf page 1, numerator column 3, denominator row 28: 2.95 (lightface) and 4.57 (boldface). Reject the null that all three coefficients are zero; R gives P = 9.43e-07.

steps.title: Test each coefficient
steps.words: Compare each magnitude with t_0.05(28) = 2.048 (t_table.pdf page 1, row 28). Age and Exercise exceed it; BMI does not (P = 0.554), so BMI is not significant.

steps.title: Confirm with the 95% intervals
steps.words: The by-hand BMI interval matches confint() to rounding. It contains zero, while the Age and Exercise intervals do not, which agrees with the t tests.

steps.title: Refit without BMI
steps.words: The refit coefficients change slightly because BMI no longer shares the explanation. Both remaining t values (-5.671 and 5.345 on 29 df) exceed 3.659, the 0.001 cutoff, so P < 0.001.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute age 68 and 4.5 hours of exercise into the refit equation.

cases.conclusion: The model as a whole is significant (F = 18.21 on 3 and 28 df, P < 0.01). Age and Exercise are significant (P < 0.001) but BMI is not (t = 0.598, CI includes 0). The refit gives ŷ = 606.1512 − 3.2801·Age + 14.5800·Exercise, and the predicted mean distance for a 68-year-old exercising 4.5 h/week is 448.71 m.

cases.title: Probability and odds of CHD at age 60
cases.context: Hosmer and Lemeshow data: age and presence of coronary heart disease (CHD) for 100 subjects. R fits glm(CHD ~ AGE, family = "binomial") by maximum likelihood.
tasks: Test whether age is related to the probability of CHD using the z value for AGE.
Calculate the probability of CHD for a 60-year-old.
Calculate the odds of CHD at age 60 and state them as odds to 1.

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability of CHD does not change with age.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability of CHD changes with age.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (age in years), \(p\) (probability of CHD), \(z\) (estimate divided by its standard error).

steps.title: Test the age coefficient
steps.words: Use the infinity row of t_table.pdf, page 2, for the Normal cutoffs: 1.960 at 0.05 and 3.2905 at 0.001. Reject with P < 0.001; R prints 4.02e-06.

steps.title: Form the linear predictor
steps.words: The linear predictor is the logit, the natural log of the odds.

steps.title: Convert to a probability
steps.words: The logistic function keeps the result between 0 and 1. Rounded to two places, p = 0.79 as on the slide.

steps.title: Calculate the odds
steps.words: The slide divides the rounded probability 0.79 by 0.21 and gets 3.76. Carrying p unrounded gives 3.84; rounding p to two places causes the difference.

cases.conclusion: Age is a significant predictor of CHD (z = 4.610, P < 0.001). A 60-year-old has an estimated CHD probability of 0.7934 (0.79), and odds of about 3.76:1 from the rounded probability (3.84:1 unrounded).

cases.title: O-ring failure and launch temperature
cases.context: Devore data: O-ring failure (Y/N) and launch temperature (°F) for 24 shuttle launches before the Challenger accident in January 1986. R fits glm(Failure ~ Temp, family = "binomial").
tasks: Test whether launch temperature is related to the probability of O-ring failure.
Calculate the probability of failure at 53 °F and at 75 °F.
Calculate the factor by which the odds of failure change for each 1 °F increase.

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability of O-ring failure does not change with launch temperature.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability of O-ring failure changes with launch temperature.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (launch temperature, °F), \(p\) (probability of failure), \(e^{b_1}\) (odds multiplier per degree).

steps.title: Test the temperature coefficient
steps.words: The magnitude just exceeds the 0.05 Normal cutoff (t_table.pdf page 2, infinity row) but not the 0.02 cutoff, so 0.02 < P < 0.05; R prints 0.0493.

steps.title: Probability at 53 °F
steps.words: At the coldest launch in the data the estimated failure probability is about 0.83.

steps.title: Probability at 75 °F
steps.words: A warm launch has a much lower estimated failure probability, about 0.14.

steps.title: Odds multiplier per degree
steps.words: Each 1 °F increase multiplies the odds of failure by about 0.856, a 14% decrease in the odds.

cases.conclusion: Temperature is a significant predictor of O-ring failure (z = -1.966, 0.02 < P < 0.05). The estimated failure probability is 0.834 at 53 °F and 0.143 at 75 °F, and the odds of failure fall by a factor of 0.856 per degree.

sampleQuestions.stem: For the original campus survey (300 of 500 first-year and 240 of 480 senior students), what is the 95% margin of error for the difference in proportions using the pooled standard error?
sampleQuestions.why: The margin is 1.960 times the pooled standard error 0.03178, which is 0.0623. Using the unpooled SE, the 0.10 cutoff 1.645, or the SE alone gives the other values.

sampleQuestions.stem: For the same campus survey, what is the pooled proportion used in the standard error?
sampleQuestions.why: The pooled proportion adds the yes answers and the respondents across both groups: 540/980 = 0.5510. Averaging the two proportions gives 0.5500, which ignores the unequal group sizes.

sampleQuestions.stem: In the hormone replacement therapy table (574 of 9,057 hormone users and 2,051 of 19,571 never-users died), what is the relative risk of dying for the hormone group?
sampleQuestions.why: RR divides the hormone-group death proportion 0.06338 by the never-used proportion 0.10480. Inverting, using raw counts, or using the odds ratio gives the other values.

sampleQuestions.stem: For the hormone therapy 2×2 table, what is the Yates-corrected chi-square statistic?
sampleQuestions.why: Subtracting one half from each |O − E| before squaring gives 127.06; without the correction it is 127.55. The values 3.841 and 10.828 are the table cutoffs, not the statistic.

sampleQuestions.stem: For the hormone therapy table, what is the expected number of deaths in the hormone group if both groups had the same death rate?
sampleQuestions.why: Expected count = (row total 9,057)(column total 2,625)/28,628 = 830.47 deaths, well above the 574 observed.

sampleQuestions.stem: For the Plutonian slope comparison (male slope 3.2833, SE 0.2041; female slope 2.0290, SE 0.4708), what is the standard error of the slope difference?
sampleQuestions.why: Square both standard errors, add, and take the root: √(0.04166 + 0.22165) = 0.51314. Adding the SEs themselves, subtracting them, or forgetting the root gives the other values.

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the t statistic for equal male and female Plutonian slopes?
sampleQuestions.why: t = 1.2543/0.51314 = 2.444. The other values use the wrong denominator or test one slope against zero.

sampleQuestions.stem: How many degrees of freedom does the Plutonian slope comparison use, and what is the two-sided 0.05 cutoff?
sampleQuestions.why: ν = 18 + 18 − 4 = 32, and row 32 of the printed t table gives 2.037 in the 0.05 column.
